To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the implementation of a structured approach of antimicrobial management (SAAAM) in a hospital setting can reduce the duration of antimicrobial therapy and can reduce hospital length of stay (LOS) without an increase in adverse events.

(1) the use of a structured approach for the management of antimicrobial therapy in the hospital can reduce antibiotic consumption by 10-20%; (2) this reduction is associated with a significant reduction in the number of days of antibiotic use per patient, and (3) the reduction of antibiotic consumption is associated with a reduction of the number of days in hospital.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the following questions: What is the role of the hospital in antibiotic stewardship?
the development of a novel approach to antimicrobial stewardship that will improve patient outcomes, reduce antimicrobial resistance and reduce costs.
antibiotic stewardship and early hospital discharge.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the use of antibiotics for the treatment of acute bacterial sinusitis should be limited to those patients who present with severe or persistent symptoms, those who have failed to respond to initial antibiotic treatment, those who present with complications of acute sinusitis and those who present with a severe or complicated course of the disease.
the use of antibiotics in the treatment of acute sinusitis is not supported by the evidence.
antibiotic stewardship is an important part of a comprehensive approach to antimicrobial use.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
antibiotic stewardship programs are effective at improving antibiotic use in hospitals and in preventing the spread of antibiotic resistance.

the antibiotic stewardship team at the hospital was able to reduce the number of days that patients were on antibiotics by 10% and the number of days of antibiotic therapy per patient by 5% without increasing the number of readmissions or the length of stay in the hospital.
we are developing a new approach to the management of patients who have a fever and neutropenia.
The main takeaway from our work is that
we need to do a better job of communicating the risks and benefits of antibiotics to patients and families.
we can safely and effectively discharge patients from the hospital earlier with a structured approach to the management of antibiotics.
we can reduce antibiotic use by 50-60% in hospitals by following a simple, structured approach to antibiotic management.
